title: New data suggests smart peptide-based materials may be an effective way to treat and prevent caries
html:
6ada64d6b50f5a7bc05888e4 Gettyimages2279150263

A recent study from The Journal of The American Dental Association (JADA) investigated the efficacy of smart-peptide based materials for caries management, which affects 2 billion people worldwide according to the World Health Organization.1

Such a widespread health burden has prompted researchers to explore more effective solutions, especially in recent years as treatment has shifted from a drill-and-fill approach towards modern, less invasive modalities. However, the downsides of common treatment options available today underscore the need for a safer alternative with higher efficacy rates and fewer side effects. 

Why current treatment options are not enough 

Fluoride: According to two clinical studies cited in JADA, fluoride is “limited in its ability to reverse deeper caries lesions and exhibits only modest antimicrobial effects, as mineral deposition at the surface can hinder repair of subsurface lesions.”1 

  • Silver diamine fluoride: Even with its dual antibacterial and remineralizing properties,silver diamine fluoride can stain teeth and cause a metallic taste in the mouth. 

Chlorhexidine: Although effective as an antimicrobial tool, chlorhexidine drastically alters a patient’s oral microbiome and can lead to tooth staining and taste alteration, making it undesirable for long-time use. 

The benefits of peptides for caries treatment 

Naturally occurring antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are unique in their biocompatibility for caries treatment; they are produced by the oral cavity to fight pathogens and do not disrupt the oral microbiome in the process (thus eliminating the risk for antimicrobial resistance). 

By modifying the peptides’ natural templates, scientists can generate smart peptides that: “recognize cariogenic conditions, such as acidic pH, pathogenic bacteria, or demineralized tooth surfaces.” This paves the way for a personalized caries management solution that does not threaten the oral microbiome in the process. 

JADA's exploration into AMPs as a future treatment option focused on their ability to perform three essential tasks: prevent lesion formation, arrest progressing lesions, and promote remineralization of early demineralized tissue.  

Study results and a glimpse into the future 

Researchers found that AMPs' ability to target demineralized tooth surfaces represent a promising component of caries therapy because they can restore damaged tissues instead of just suppressing cariogenic microorganisms. 
 

The principal approaches studied by researchers were: 

Mineral-guiding peptides: Direct and organize hydroxyapatite formation 

Ion-binding peptides: Recruit calcium and phosphate to damaged surfaces 

Scaffold-forming peptides: Create three-dimensional templates for mineral nucleation and growth

Cell-activating peptides: Stimulate endogenous dentin matrix production and physiological repair 

However, a single-functioning AMP may not be enough to address the three previously mentioned aspects of caries management. Therefore, Aan integrated multifunctional peptide system may be a more promising solution which is something researchers are currently developing.  

Such a system would combine two or more therapeutic elements of smart peptides.

Ideally, it would be able to perform the following tasks: 

  • Suppress cariogenic bacteria and biofilm formation 

  • Target and retain therapeutic peptides on enamel surfaces 

  • Promote mineral deposition and restore tooth structure 

  • Improve efficacy of antimicrobial agents

  • Provide sustained or concentration-dependent therapeutic effects 

Translating research into clinical practice 

If successful, researchers concluded that future development of multifunctional smart peptide systems: “may enable personalized, microbiome-sparing, and lesion-specific interventions in routine oral health care.”1

This would help patients requiring long-term antimicrobial (those with xerostomia, undergoing head and neck radiotherapy, or taking medications that increase caries risk) support can benefit from smart peptide systems because they can alter the microbiome without destroying it. Smart peptides would also benefit those at an increased risk for developing caries overall (older adults, medically compromised patients, those with reduced salivary functions). 

Smart peptides are minimally invasive too; they can be applied via varnish, gel, or through a mouthwash. In restorative dentistry, they can be added to adhesives, liners, or other restorative materials. Research noted that this may also help prevent secondary caries, which is a common side effect of restoration failure. 

Overall, smart peptides show significant clinical promise as a way to not only treat but prevent dental caries. According to JADA authors, “realizing their clinical potential will require coordinated advances in peptide engineering, delivery system design, and rigorous clinical evaluation.”1

Reference: 

  1. Fu Y, Cannon RD, Cheng L, Li KC, Ekambaram M, Cooper PR, Mei ML. Smart peptide-based materials and their clinical application for caries management. J Am Dent Assoc. 2026;157(10):1105-1117. doi:10.1016/j.adaj.2026.07.002
